subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage: At the club pool in Pune, Manav sat on the edge with wet feet and watched Zeenat, the older girl in lane three, cut through the water. Her right arm swung up, her hand slid in, and she pulled. Manav stood on the tiles and copied the movement, arm over arm, in the air. Then he tried it in the water while Bhavna Ma'am walked along the side. "Good reach. Your elbow is dropping, Manav. Lift it first, like Zeenat does." He lifted it. The stroke felt strange, but the splash was smaller, and he managed a full length without stopping.

qa.q: Whose arm movement did Manav watch before trying the stroke?
qa.a: He watched Zeenat, the older girl in lane three.

qa.q: What was Manav feeling as he tried the stroke in the water with the coach beside him?
qa.a: Curious and a little unsure, because the stroke felt strange, yet he kept going and was pleased when the splash got smaller. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could help Manav see his own elbow, and why?
qa.a: A friend could film a short clip from the poolside, so Manav can watch his elbow and fix it between lessons.

qa.q: How does Bhavna Ma'am see Manav's copying?
qa.a: She sees a good start, since he already has the rough shape of the stroke, and she adds the one missing correction about his elbow.

grounding: A boy studies an older swimmer, copies the arm movement on land and in the water, and the coach corrects his elbow.

subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage:
"Avni ma'am, look at that boy in lane four. His arms go so smooth."
"That's front crawl. What do you notice?"
"His hand goes in near his head. Then it pushes back all the way to his leg."
"Good. Try it here, standing on the poolside."
Joseph swung his arms, one after the other.
"Now in the water. I'm watching."
He pushed off and swung his arms the same way. Water splashed everywhere.
"Stop. Joseph, your elbow is straight, like a windmill. His elbow bends and stays high. Try again."
"Like this?"
"Higher. Yes. Feel the difference?"
"It's quieter. And I'm faster!"

qa.q: Which lane was the older swimmer in?
How did Joseph feel when he said, "It's quieter. And I'm faster!"?
qa.a: He felt excited and pleased, noticing the difference the bent elbow made.

qa.q: What else could Joseph do to keep improving his stroke?
qa.a: He could practise one arm at a time holding a float, because focusing on one arm makes the elbow easier to control.

qa.q: How does Joseph's copying look to Avni ma'am?
qa.a: Avni ma'am is happy he is watching carefully, and sees that copying works best when she checks and corrects it.

grounding: It shows a boy watching an older swimmer's arm movement, copying it on the poolside and in the water, and the coach fixing his elbow.

subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage: At the club pool I watched the older swimmers for a whole week before I tried anything. One boy's arms fascinated me. They came out of the water bent at the elbow, reached forward, went in without a splash. On Saturday I stood on the poolside and copied him slowly in the air. Right arm, left arm, head to the side to breathe. Then I got in and tried it with Anand sir watching. "Your elbow is dropping, Jomon," he said. "Keep it high, like you're reaching over a fence." I tried again. It felt awkward, then it felt right. I'm still slow, but now my arms look a little like his, and I don't splash the whole lane.

qa.q: What did Anand sir say was dropping?
qa.a: He said Jomon's elbow was dropping.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when the new movement first felt awkward?
qa.a: Jomon felt unsure and a bit clumsy, and then pleased when it started to feel right.

qa.q: What else could Jomon try to check his arms without a coach?
qa.a: Jomon could ask a friend to take a short video at the poolside, so the elbow can be checked later.

qa.q: How might the older swimmer see Jomon copying him?
qa.a: The older swimmer might be surprised or flattered that someone was watching his stroke so closely.
